questions.stem: In the Commonwealth Parliament, the role of the Crown in law-making is carried out by:
options: the Governor-General, who gives royal assent to bills passed by both Houses
the Prime Minister, who signs each bill into law once it passes the lower House
the Chief Justice of the High Court, who approves bills before they are debated
the Speaker of the House, who decides which bills are presented to the monarch
questions.explanation: The Governor-General represents the Crown at the Commonwealth level and gives royal assent, which turns a bill into an Act. The Prime Minister leads the government but has no power to give assent.

questions.stem: Which person gives royal assent to bills passed by the Victorian Parliament?
options: The Victorian Speaker
The Governor of Victoria
The Premier of Victoria
The Governor-General
questions.explanation: The Governor of Victoria represents the Crown in the state and gives royal assent to bills passed by both Houses of the Victorian Parliament. The Governor-General performs this role only for Commonwealth bills.

questions.stem: By convention, the Governor-General gives royal assent to bills on the advice of the government. Which statement best describes the practical effect of this?
options: Royal assent is given only after the High Court confirms that the bill is constitutional
Royal assent is in practice a formality for a bill that both Houses have passed
The Governor-General regularly refuses assent to bills that are opposed by much of the public
The Governor-General can amend a bill before giving assent if it contains drafting errors
questions.explanation: By convention the Crown's representative acts on the advice of ministers, so assent to a bill passed by both Houses is in practice a formality and is not withheld. The Governor-General cannot amend a bill, and the High Court does not check bills before assent.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of the House of Representatives in law-making?
options: It is the house of review, in which each state is represented by an equal number of members
It is the house that gives royal assent to bills after they have been passed by the Senate
It is the house that interprets legislation when disputes arise about the meaning of words
It is the house in which government is formed and in which most bills are introduced
questions.explanation: The party or coalition with the support of a majority in the House of Representatives forms government, and most bills, including all money bills, start there. Equal state representation is a feature of the Senate.

questions.stem: Why is the Senate often described as a house of review and a states' house?
options: It scrutinises bills passed by the lower house, and each original state elects the same number of senators
It reviews High Court decisions on appeal, and each state's senators are chosen by that state's own government
It decides which bills become law without debate, and each state is represented according to population
It reviews the decisions of the Governor-General, and each state's premier sits in it as a member
questions.explanation: The Senate reviews, debates and can amend or reject bills from the House of Representatives, and each original state has equal representation regardless of population. Senators are elected by the people of their state, not appointed by state governments.

questions.stem: The Senate wishes to change a bill imposing a new tax. Under section 53 of the Constitution, which statement is correct?
options: The Senate cannot consider the bill at all, because tax bills need only pass the House of Representatives
The Senate may amend the bill only if the High Court confirms the tax is within the Commonwealth's power
The Senate cannot amend the bill, but it may return it to the House of Representatives requesting amendments
The Senate may amend the bill freely, but it must first obtain the Governor-General's written permission to do so
questions.explanation: Section 53 stops the Senate from originating or amending bills imposing taxation, but it may request amendments and can still reject such a bill. Every bill, including a tax bill, must pass both Houses before it receives assent.

questions.stem: In the Victorian Parliament, the Legislative Council's main role in law-making is to:
options: give royal assent to bills passed by the Legislative Assembly on behalf of the Crown
hear appeals against the validity of laws made by the Victorian Legislative Assembly
act as a house of review, debating and possibly amending bills passed by the Legislative Assembly
form the government and introduce most bills, including the annual budget bills that fund the state
questions.explanation: The Legislative Council is Victoria's upper house and acts as a house of review. Government is formed in the Legislative Assembly, where most bills start, and royal assent is given by the Governor.

questions.stem: Residual powers are law-making powers that:
options: are transferred to the High Court after a successful referendum
are not listed in the Constitution and remain with the states
are listed in section 51 and may be used by both parliaments
are given only to the Commonwealth Parliament by the Constitution
questions.explanation: Residual powers were left with the states because the Constitution does not list them, such as criminal law and public transport. Powers listed in section 51 that both parliaments can use are concurrent powers.

questions.stem: The power to make laws about currency and coinage is best classified as:
options: a residual power of the state parliaments
a power held only by the Reserve Bank
an exclusive power of the Commonwealth Parliament
a concurrent power shared by both parliaments
questions.explanation: Currency is listed in section 51, and section 115 forbids the states from coining money, which makes the power exclusive to the Commonwealth. A section 51 power is only concurrent when the states are not also prevented from using it.

questions.stem: Both the Victorian and Commonwealth parliaments make laws imposing taxes, such as land tax and income tax. Taxation (other than customs and excise duties) is therefore an example of:
options: a concurrent power
an exclusive power
a residual power
a referred power
questions.explanation: Taxation is listed in section 51 and both levels may use it, so it is concurrent. Customs and excise duties are excluded because section 90 makes them exclusive to the Commonwealth.

questions.stem: Which law could most likely be made only by the Victorian Parliament, using a residual power?
options: A law setting the speed limits that apply on Victorian roads
A law establishing a new Australian Defence Force regiment
A law setting the rate of customs duty on imported cars
A law creating a new coin as legal tender in Australia
questions.explanation: Road rules are not listed in the Constitution, so they fall within the states' residual powers. Defence forces, customs duties and coinage are all exclusive Commonwealth powers.

questions.stem: Which pair of constitutional sections together makes the power to raise armed forces exclusive to the Commonwealth?
options: Section 90, which covers customs and excise, and section 109, which resolves inconsistent laws
Section 128, which sets out the referendum process, and section 7, which covers the composition of the Senate
Section 51(vi), the defence power, and section 114, which bars states from raising naval or military forces
Section 51(xxix), the external affairs power, and section 116, which bars states from establishing a religion
questions.explanation: Defence is a section 51 head of power, and section 114 prevents states raising naval or military forces without Commonwealth consent, so the power is exclusive. Section 116 restricts the Commonwealth, not the states.

questions.stem: Victoria wants to impose its own duty on goods imported into the state through the Port of Melbourne. Why would such a law be invalid?
options: Section 116 forbids states from imposing any new tax without a referendum
Section 7 requires the Senate to approve every tax imposed by a state parliament
Section 90 makes customs duties an exclusive power of the Commonwealth
Section 109 makes every state tax invalid once the Commonwealth taxes income
questions.explanation: Section 90 gives the Commonwealth exclusive power over customs and excise duties, so a state cannot impose a duty on imports. Section 109 only applies when a valid state law conflicts with a Commonwealth law; states can still impose other taxes, such as land tax.

questions.stem: Section 109 of the Constitution provides that:
options: where a state law covers a residual power, the Commonwealth Parliament may veto it within six months of royal assent
where a state law is inconsistent with a Commonwealth law, the Commonwealth law prevails to the extent of the inconsistency
where a Commonwealth law is inconsistent with a state law, the more recent of the two laws prevails in every case
where two state laws are inconsistent with each other, the High Court decides which one of them should apply
questions.explanation: Section 109 resolves conflicts between valid state and Commonwealth laws: the Commonwealth law prevails and the state law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency. Which law was passed first is irrelevant.

questions.stem: A Victorian law sets the minimum age for a particular licence at 18, while a valid Commonwealth law on the same matter sets it at 16. A 17-year-old applies. What is the effect of section 109?
options: The applicant may choose which of the two laws to follow, because both laws are valid
The Commonwealth law prevails, and the Victorian law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency
The Victorian law prevails, because it was passed by the parliament closest to the applicant's home
Both laws are invalid, because two parliaments cannot make laws on the same subject
questions.explanation: The Victorian law would take away what the Commonwealth law allows a 17-year-old to do, so the laws are inconsistent and the Commonwealth law prevails under section 109. Both parliaments can legislate on concurrent matters; section 109 only matters when their laws conflict.

questions.stem: Why is section 109 significant in a federal system?
options: It resolves conflicts in areas of concurrent power, giving certainty about which law applies
It prevents the states from making any laws on subjects listed in section 51 of the Constitution
It allows a state law to override a Commonwealth law if the people of that state approve it
It gives the High Court the power to rewrite inconsistent laws so that they are consistent
questions.explanation: Because both parliaments can legislate in concurrent areas, conflicts are inevitable, and section 109 settles them in favour of the Commonwealth. States can still make laws on section 51 matters as long as they are not inconsistent with Commonwealth law.

questions.stem: In the Tasmanian Dam case (Commonwealth v Tasmania, 1983), the High Court held that the Commonwealth could stop the Franklin Dam by relying on the:
options: trade and commerce power, to regulate the sale of electricity
external affairs power, to implement the World Heritage Convention
defence power, to protect the dam site as a military training area
taxation power, to impose a heavy tax on building the dam itself
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth passed a law implementing Australia's obligations under the World Heritage Convention, and the High Court held, four to three, that it was valid under the external affairs power in section 51(xxix). The decision did not rely on defence, taxation or trade powers.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the impact of the Tasmanian Dam case on law-making powers?
options: It removed the states' residual powers over land use and gave them all to the Commonwealth after a referendum
It ruled that a state law prevails over a Commonwealth law when it concerns natural resources
It expanded the Commonwealth's power, allowing it to legislate on matters such as the environment through treaties
It reduced the Commonwealth's power, confirming that environmental protection is a state matter only
questions.explanation: By upholding a law implementing an international treaty, the case showed that the external affairs power lets the Commonwealth legislate in areas, such as the environment, that are not otherwise listed in the Constitution. The constitutional text was not changed, as only a referendum could do that.

questions.stem: In the Tasmanian Dam case, the Tasmanian law authorising the dam ceased to operate once the High Court upheld the Commonwealth law. Which constitutional provision explains this?
options: Section 53, because the state law had imposed a tax without Senate approval
Section 109, because the state law was inconsistent with a valid Commonwealth law
Section 128, because the people of Tasmania voted to repeal the state law
Section 116, because the dam interfered with the free exercise of religion
questions.explanation: Once the Commonwealth law was held valid, the Tasmanian law authorising the dam was inconsistent with it, so section 109 made the Commonwealth law prevail. There was no referendum, and sections 116 and 53 were not in issue.

questions.stem: A government holds a majority in both Houses of Parliament. Which is the most likely effect on law-making?
options: Bills may pass quickly with less scrutiny, as the upper house may act as a rubber stamp
Bills will take longer to pass, because the upper house must reject them at least once
Bills cannot pass without a referendum, because the upper house has lost its review role
Bills must be approved by the High Court, because the upper house cannot act as a check
questions.explanation: When the government controls both Houses, the upper house is less able to act as a house of review, so laws can pass quickly but with weaker scrutiny. Neither a referendum nor the High Court has any role in approving ordinary bills.

questions.stem: The government lacks a majority in the upper house, and crossbench members insist on amendments before supporting a bill. How does this feature of a bicameral parliament affect law-making?
options: It means the bill can be passed by the lower house alone after a short period of delay
It means the High Court must decide whether the amendments are in the public interest
It can improve laws through scrutiny and compromise, but it can also delay or block reform
It means the bill must be decided by the Governor-General, who then rules on each amendment
questions.explanation: A bicameral structure lets the upper house review and amend bills, which can produce better-considered laws, but the need to negotiate can slow reform or stop it altogether. The Governor-General and the High Court have no role in resolving such negotiations.

questions.stem: After Australia signs an international treaty, other countries and United Nations bodies urge Australia to pass laws to meet its obligations. This is an example of:
options: the separation of the executive and judicial powers in the Constitution
section 109 resolving an inconsistency between two parliaments' laws
international pressures affecting the ability of parliament to make law
the High Court protecting the principle of representative government
questions.explanation: Treaties and the views of the international community can pressure parliament to legislate, or to change laws, in line with global standards. Representative government and the separation of powers concern how the Constitution checks parliament, not outside pressure.

questions.stem: Why can the representative nature of parliament limit its ability to make law?
options: Members cannot introduce any bill unless a majority of voters first sign a petition
Members must follow High Court rulings on which policies the community supports
Members may avoid controversial reforms that could cost them votes at the next election
Members are appointed by the Crown, so they cannot act on the views of the voters
questions.explanation: Members of parliament want to be re-elected, so they may hesitate to pass laws that could be unpopular with large groups of voters, even if those laws are needed. Members are elected by the people, not appointed, and need no petition to introduce a bill.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason that a parliament's representative nature can be a strength in law-making?
options: Members serve for life, so they can pass laws without concern about the next election
Members are not bound by the Constitution, so they can make laws on any subject
Members are accountable to voters, so laws tend to reflect the values of the majority
Members are judges chosen for their expertise, so laws are always technically correct
questions.explanation: Because members must face elections, they have a strong incentive to make laws that reflect community values. Members are not judges, serve fixed terms and are bound by the Constitution.

questions.stem: The Victorian Parliament is described as bicameral because it:
options: needs the approval of both the Governor and the Premier for every new law
has two Houses, the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council
shares its law-making powers with the Commonwealth under section 51
has two levels of government, state and local, that pass its laws together
questions.explanation: Bicameral means having two Houses, which in Victoria are the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council. Local councils make by-laws under state legislation, but they are not a House of the Victorian Parliament.

questions.stem: Sections 7 and 24 of the Constitution require that members of the Senate and the House of Representatives be:
options: appointed by the state premiers
approved by the High Court
nominated by the Governor-General
directly chosen by the people
questions.explanation: Sections 7 and 24 say senators and members of the House of Representatives must be directly chosen by the people, which is the basis of representative government. The High Court has used these words to protect voting rights and political communication.

questions.stem: In Roach v Electoral Commissioner (2007), the High Court held that a Commonwealth law removing the right to vote from all prisoners was invalid. Why?
options: It was inconsistent with a Victorian law allowing prisoners to vote in state elections
It was inconsistent with the express right to trial by jury in section 80
It was inconsistent with the requirement that parliament be directly chosen by the people
It was inconsistent with the express right to freedom of religion in section 116
questions.explanation: The High Court found that a blanket ban on prisoner voting was not reconcilable with sections 7 and 24, which require parliament to be directly chosen by the people. The earlier rule disqualifying prisoners serving three years or more remained valid.

questions.stem: In the Australian Capital Television case (1992), the High Court struck down a Commonwealth ban on political advertising on radio and television during election periods. On what basis?
options: The Constitution contains an implied freedom of political communication arising from representative government
The Constitution contains an express right to freedom of speech set out in section 116
The ban was inconsistent with state electoral laws and so was invalid under section 109
The ban had been made by the executive government by regulation, without ever being passed by parliament
questions.explanation: The High Court found an implied freedom of political communication, because voters must be able to discuss political matters to make a real choice under sections 7 and 24. The Constitution has no express right to free speech, and section 116 concerns religion.

questions.stem: The principle of representative government means that:
options: parliament must pass every law that a majority of voters ask for in a petition
parliament is made up of members appointed to represent each industry and profession
parliament must include an equal number of members from every state and territory
parliament is made up of members elected by the people, who are accountable to them
questions.explanation: Representative government means the people elect members of parliament to make laws on their behalf, and those members can be voted out. Members are not obliged to follow petitions, and only the Senate gives equal representation, to the original states.

questions.stem: Under the separation of powers in the Constitution, judicial power is exercised by:
options: the Attorney-General and the public service
the High Court and other federal courts
the Governor-General and the ministers
the Senate and the House of Representatives
questions.explanation: Chapter III vests judicial power in the High Court and other federal courts. Executive power lies with the Governor-General and ministers, and legislative power with the Parliament.

questions.stem: How does the separation of the judicial power act as a check on parliament?
options: Parliament can direct judges on how to decide cases involving its own laws
Independent courts can rule that a law made beyond parliament's powers is invalid
Judges sit in parliament and can vote against bills they believe are unconstitutional
Courts must approve each bill before it is passed by both Houses of Parliament
questions.explanation: Because the courts are independent of parliament, they can declare a law ultra vires if it goes beyond constitutional limits. Judges do not sit in parliament or approve bills, and parliament cannot direct how a case is decided.

questions.stem: Which statement about the separation of powers in Australia is most accurate?
options: All three powers are kept completely separate, so government ministers are not allowed to be members of parliament
The executive and judicial powers overlap, because ministers sit as judges in the High Court
The legislative and judicial powers overlap, because the High Court can introduce bills into parliament
The legislative and executive powers overlap, because ministers sit in parliament, but judicial power is kept separate
questions.explanation: Under responsible government, ministers who exercise executive power must be members of parliament, so these two powers overlap. The courts, however, are kept strictly separate, which protects their independence.

questions.stem: In the Boilermakers' case (1956), the High Court held that a body exercising federal judicial power cannot also exercise non-judicial power. What does this case show?
options: The Constitution lets courts make laws through statutory interpretation alone
The Constitution places the executive under the control of the High Court
The Constitution keeps judicial power strictly separate from the other powers
The Constitution allows parliament to give judicial power to any public body
questions.explanation: The Boilermakers' case confirmed that federal judicial power must be exercised only by Chapter III courts, and that those courts cannot be given non-judicial functions. This strict separation helps the courts act as an independent check.

questions.stem: Which right is expressly protected by the Australian Constitution?
options: Freedom of speech, under section 41
Freedom of assembly, under section 80
The right to privacy, under section 117
Freedom of religion, under section 116
questions.explanation: Section 116 prevents the Commonwealth from establishing a religion, imposing religious observance, prohibiting the free exercise of religion or requiring a religious test for office. The Constitution has no express rights to free speech, assembly or privacy.

questions.stem: The Commonwealth compulsorily acquires a farm to build an airport. Under section 51(xxxi), the owner is entitled to:
options: an exemption from the law
acquisition on just terms
a referendum on the issue
a trial by jury on the matter
questions.explanation: Section 51(xxxi) allows the Commonwealth to acquire property only on just terms, which usually means fair compensation. The other options are not protections attached to the acquisition of property.

questions.stem: In Street v Queensland Bar Association (1989), Queensland rules made it harder for barristers who lived interstate to practise in Queensland. The High Court held these rules invalid under:
options: section 51(xxxi), which protects people's property from acquisition without just terms
section 117, which protects against discrimination based on state of residence
section 116, which protects the free exercise of religion from interference
section 80, which protects trial by jury for offences against Commonwealth law
questions.explanation: Section 117 prevents a resident of one state from being discriminated against in another state because of where they live, and the residence rules breached it. It is one of the few express rights that binds the states as well as the Commonwealth.

questions.stem: A Victorian law requires all public servants to declare their religion. A student argues that section 116 makes the law invalid. Why is the student most likely wrong?
options: Section 116 applies only to criminal trials held in the High Court of Australia
Section 116 restricts the Commonwealth Parliament and does not apply to the states
Section 116 protects only those religions that were recognised in Australia in 1901
Section 116 can be suspended by any parliament that passes a law with a two-thirds majority
questions.explanation: The words of section 116 begin ‘The Commonwealth shall not make any law’, so it does not limit state parliaments. This narrowness is one reason express rights are said to provide limited protection.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the express protection of rights as a check on parliament?
options: The rights are protected by the Governor-General, who can refuse assent to any law that might breach them
The rights are entrenched and can only be removed by referendum, but there are few of them and they are narrowly interpreted
The rights are extensive and cover all civil liberties, but parliament may override any of them by passing ordinary legislation
The rights are found in a Charter that the High Court can amend, but they apply only when parliament agrees
questions.explanation: Express rights are entrenched in the Constitution, so parliament cannot remove them by ordinary legislation, which makes them a strong check. However, there are only a handful and the courts have read some, such as section 41, narrowly.

questions.stem: Section 80 of the Constitution is described as an express right. It provides that:
options: every adult resident of Australia has the right to vote at all elections
the Commonwealth shall not make any law imposing a religious observance
the trial on indictment of an offence against a Commonwealth law shall be by jury
every person charged with any offence in any court has the right to a lawyer
questions.explanation: Section 80 guarantees trial by jury for trials on indictment of offences against Commonwealth law. It does not give a right to a lawyer, and the right to vote is not protected in such broad terms.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the High Court's protection of representative government is a significant check on parliament?
options: The Court can dissolve parliament and call an election when it finds a law unpopular
The Court can refuse to hear any case that challenges a law made by parliament
The Court can approve which candidates may stand for election to parliament
The Court can strike down laws that undermine voters' ability to choose their representatives
questions.explanation: By enforcing sections 7 and 24 and the implied freedom of political communication, the High Court can invalidate laws, as in Roach and Australian Capital Television, that interfere with the people's choice. The Court cannot dissolve parliament or approve candidates.
